CDK2/cyclin A2 inhibitors: chemotype map and affinity landscape

All BindingDB compounds with a measured Ki against the wild-type CDK2/cyclin A2 complex, projected by Morgan-fingerprint similarity and annotated by chemotype and potency.

Source: BindingDB · complex targets 97 and 92 (Cyclin-A2/CDK2) · generated 3 October 2026

165compounds with Ki
13chemotypes
2.9 nMstrongest Ki
12bounded (>) values
15source publications

0The prompt

1. Retrieve compounds that bind CDK2/cyclin A2 and have Ki data.
2. Present the compounds in t-SNE plot using a Morgan fingerprint and annotate chemotypes. Create two plots, one annotate the chemotypes and one annotate by Ki.
3. For each chemotype, plot the top 3 compounds in a 3xn grid.
4. Create a .html file that includes the prompt.

1Retrieving the compounds

BindingDB stores CDK2/cyclin A2 as a protein complex rather than a single polymer, so the query targets the complex records directly: complexid 97 (Cyclin-A2/Cyclin-dependent kinase 2) and complexid 92 (the Cyclin-A2 [171–432] construct of the same pair). Mutant constructs (F82H, L83V/H84D, K89T …), the CDK1 complex, and the mixed Cyclin-A1/A2 record were excluded so that every point is the same wild-type target. Rows were filtered to affinity_type = 'Ki' and collapsed to one value per compound — the median where a compound was measured more than once. Of 165 compounds, 12 have Ki reported only as a lower bound (> 2.5–13 µM); those are drawn as open marks and excluded from "top 3" rankings.

2Chemical-space map

Each molecule is described by a Morgan (ECFP4-like) fingerprint, radius 2, folded to 2048 bits. Pairwise Tanimoto distances feed a t-SNE with a precomputed metric (perplexity 15, 2000 iterations, seed 42), so proximity on the map means fingerprint similarity and nothing else — axes carry no units and distances between well-separated clusters are not quantitative.

Chemotypes were assigned by first clustering the fingerprints (Butina, Tanimoto cutoff 0.55) to discover the natural families, then encoding each family as a substructure query built from its own Bemis–Murcko scaffold. Every one of the 165 compounds matches exactly one chemotype; none fell through to "unassigned". Seven chemotypes carry a colour; the remaining six, all with four members or fewer, share a grey fill and are separated by marker shape.

4Time-structured map (IRIS)

Create another plot using the same fingerprint and chemotype annotation using the IRIS method (https://github.com/BIDS-Xu-Lab/IRIS). Use a time/date stamp for each compound (publication date)

IRIS is a LargeVis-style projection that fixes each point's radius from its timestamp (earliest at the centre, latest at the rim) and learns only the angle from the high-dimensional neighbour graph. The inputs here are the same Morgan fingerprints and chemotype labels as Section 2; the timestamp is the publication date of the source article (year, month and day from BindingDB's article table — 15 distinct dates, Jul 2000 to Jun 2021).

Four implementation choices worth knowing

Distance. IRIS's neighbour search is compiled against a Euclidean Annoy index; Tanimoto is not available. I passed L2-normalised fingerprint bits, for which Euclidean ranking equals cosine ranking. Measured against true Tanimoto, this reproduces 99.3% of each compound's 15 nearest neighbours (raw bits: 88.2%).

A bug fix. The released package (iris-learn 1.0) crashes with a floating-point exception on any dataset below ~1,000 points: a progress counter in LargeVis.cpp computes (i-lo) % ((hi-lo)/100), which is a modulo by zero when a thread's share of points is under 100. I built the current upstream source with that line (and an identical one in a disabled checkpoint block) guarded by max(1, …). Neither touches the optimisation.

Time-to-radius map. IRIS auto-fits an exponent rho to spread timestamps; here it chose −1.24, which compressed 2013–2021 — 160 of 165 compounds — into the outer 13% of the radius. That fit assumes continuous timestamps and is ill-posed with 15 discrete dates, so I set rho = 0, the direct linear mapping IRIS provides. Radius vs. date: Spearman 1.000.

What it costs. With the radial axis given to time, the layout preserves 55% of each compound's 15 Tanimoto nearest neighbours, against 73% for the t-SNE. It still looks clean because chemistry and date are confounded in this set: 71% of every compound's chemical neighbours were published in the same paper. Read the map as "which series appeared when", not as a finer chemical-similarity map than Section 2.

Settings: 15 neighbours, 2 M SGD steps, other parameters at the upstream defaults (ζ = 0.1, β = 0.95, γ = 128, learning rate 1.0).
